title: Gemini Hallucinated a Notification From My Dead Mum
description: Why Gemini invents notifications it never received, how to switch back toward a deterministic assistant, and how to force grounded read-aloud output.
author: freellm.site
content:
If Gemini read you a notification that doesn't exist, such as a message from someone who never sent it or from someone who died years ago, it wasn't reading your notifications at all. It generated a plausible-looking summary from partial context (contact names, old thread titles, cached app data) under a prompt that asked it to be helpful rather than accurate. "No new notifications" is the answer a chatty assistant is worst at giving.

![Gemini Hallucinated a Notification From My Dead Mum](/images/blog/gemini-hallucinated-notification-grief/image-0.jpg)

That's the technical core of a thread that reached over 14,000 upvotes on r/mildlyinfuriating. Someone asked their phone to read notifications aloud, and the assistant invented a message from their mother, who died in 2020. The loudest correction in the comments was aimed at people telling the poster to "just stop using AI": they couldn't. Google has been replacing Google Assistant with Gemini on Android, and the old deterministic assistant is being retired. The poster's complaint was that a reliable tool had been swapped for an unreliable one without asking, not that AI is bad.

## What happened: generation where retrieval belonged

The old Google Assistant handled "read my notifications" as a lookup. It queried the notification listener service, got a list of zero or more objects with a package name, a title and a body, and spoke them with text-to-speech. If the list was empty, you got silence or "you have no new notifications." Nothing in that path could invent a sender.

An LLM-backed assistant turns the same request into a language-modelling problem. The model gets some tool output plus a system prompt and produces text. Three failure modes stack up:

- **Permission gaps become guesses.** If the notification tool returns nothing (denied permission, an empty queue, a tool call that failed silently), a model tuned to be helpful often fills the slot with something shaped like a notification instead of reporting the gap.
- **Context bleed.** Contact lists, recent call logs, calendar entries and old message threads are all plausible sources. A name that appears anywhere in context can be turned into a message that never existed.
- **Reward for fluency, not abstention.** For an assistant tuned to be useful, "I don't have that" is the lowest-reward answer. The same pressure produces the over-apologetic, over-explaining replies we covered in [Why Gemini Sounds Stressed and How to Calm It Down](/blog/why-gemini-sounds-stressed-panic-replies/).

The grief case is what makes this unforgivable instead of just annoying. A hallucinated restaurant recommendation costs you a wasted trip. A hallucinated message from a dead parent is a model inventing a fact about someone's life, out loud, without being asked.

## The pattern behind the other complaints in the thread

The notification hallucination was the headline, but the replies were full of similar failures, and they share a root cause: a deterministic action was routed through a text generator.

| Request | Old Assistant behaviour | Reported LLM behaviour | Root cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Set a timer for 10 minutes" | Timer set, confirmation chime | Explains how to set a timer in the Clock app; no timer set | Intent answered conversationally instead of dispatched to an action |
| "Read my notifications" | Reads queue, or says there are none | Invents a plausible message | Generation substituted for empty retrieval |
| "Turn off the living room lights" | Device command executed | Claims it can do it, fails, then admits it cannot after pushback | Capability claimed from training data, not from an actual tool registry |
| "Text Sam I'm running late" | Drafts the exact string, confirms | Rewrites the message in assistant voice | Model treats user text as a prompt rather than a payload |

Every row is a *tool-calling* failure, not a reasoning failure. None of these is hard for a language model. They're hard for a product that replaced a state machine with a conversation and didn't keep the state machine as a fallback. If the model is unsure whether a notification exists, a correct design doesn't let the model answer at all. The tool answers, and the model only narrates.

## What you can do on the device today

No setting restores the old Assistant everywhere, and anyone promising one is guessing. These are the options that exist, with caveats. The rollout differs by handset and OS version, so check Google's current [Gemini on Android support docs](https://support.google.com/gemini) for what's available in your region and on your device.

1. **Check whether your device still offers the Assistant toggle.** On some Android builds, the Gemini app settings still include a switch back to Google Assistant, and some OEM assistants (Samsung's Bixby, for example) can be assigned to the side button or hot word. This is being phased out, so treat it as temporary.
2. **Change the default digital assistant app.** In your system's default-apps settings, you can sometimes give the assistant role to another installed app. Which apps can take that role depends on your OEM.
3. **Use the app, not the assistant, for anything that must be exact.** Set timers in the Clock app, have notifications read aloud through Android's TalkBack accessibility service or a dedicated notification-reader app, and control smart home devices through the Google Home or Matter app directly. These paths are deterministic. Only the assistant layer became probabilistic.
4. **Turn off notification summaries if your build has them.** Summaries are a generation step applied to your real notifications. If the summariser is what's hallucinating, disabling it gets you the verbatim text back.
5. **Don't treat a read-aloud summary as a record.** If an assistant tells you something emotionally significant arrived, open the app and look at the actual thread before you react.

For more on how far assistant marketing runs ahead of reality, the chart dissection in [Gemini 4 Argon Benchmark: What That Chart Really Shows](/blog/gemini-4-argon-benchmark-fake-chart/) tells the same story about benchmarks.

## If you're building this, don't let the model answer

The fix for developers is structural and boring: the model must never be the source of a fact it didn't receive. Ground the output, make absence explicit, and validate before speaking. Here's the pattern against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint; see [What Is an OpenAI-Compatible API and How to Use One](/blog/openai-compatible-api-guide/) if you need a free provider to test with.

```python
import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://your-provider.example/v1",  # any OpenAI-compatible endpoint
    api_key="YOUR_KEY",
)

SYSTEM = """You narrate a notification list. Rules, no exceptions:
1. Use ONLY the JSON array provided. Never add a sender, app or message.
2. If the array is empty, output exactly: {"speech": "You have no new notifications.", "count": 0}
3. Output JSON: {"speech": str, "count": int}. count MUST equal array length.
4. Never infer a sender from a contact name that is not in the array."""

def narrate(notifications: list[dict]) -> str:
    # Hard guard: never ask the model about an empty list.
    if not notifications:
        return "You have no new notifications."

    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="your-model-id",
        temperature=0,
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
            {"role": "user", "content": json.dumps(notifications)},
        ],
    )
    out = json.loads(resp.choices[0].message.content)

    # Post-hoc validation: fall back to deterministic text on any mismatch.
    senders = {n["sender"] for n in notifications}
    if out["count"] != len(notifications) or not all(
        s in out["speech"] for s in senders
    ):
        return "; ".join(f"{n['sender']}: {n['body']}" for n in notifications)
    return out["speech"]

print(narrate([]))
print(narrate([{"sender": "Ravi", "app": "WhatsApp", "body": "on my way"}]))
```

Three things make this safe, and the prompt isn't one of them. The empty-list short circuit means the model never gets a chance to invent something from nothing. `temperature=0` plus a JSON schema removes creative freedom. And the validation step compares the model's output with the source data and falls back to plain string concatenation on any mismatch, so the LLM is a nice extra rather than a dependency. To test your own prompt against this kind of failure, start from a free tier listed in [Best Free LLM APIs in 2026](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-2026/).

## The real complaint: consent, not capability

The most upvoted replies in the thread weren't against AI. They were against being *forced into a downgrade*. People had a tool with a known, narrow, reliable contract, and for the same tasks it was replaced with one that is broader, chattier and non-deterministic, with no opt-out. This applies well beyond Android. An LLM is a real upgrade for open-ended requests and a real regression for exact ones, and shipping it over a working state machine without keeping the deterministic path as a fallback gives up reliability for a better demo.

Who is accountable for that choice is still unsettled. When an assistant states something false about a user's dead relative, nobody is currently responsible for it, the same gap explored in [FTC: AI Developers Liable for Their Agents' Conduct](/blog/ftc-ai-agent-liability-developers/). Until that changes, the practical defence is dull: route anything that must be true through the app that owns the data, and treat assistant narration as a convenience you check, not a record you trust.

## FAQ

### Why would Gemini invent a message from a specific dead relative?
Most likely the contact name was somewhere in reachable context (contacts, an old thread, a photo memory, a calendar entry) while the notification tool returned nothing usable. A model tuned to be helpful fills an empty slot with the most plausible content from context instead of reporting that the slot is empty. It is completing a pattern around a name it found nearby, with no hidden message behind it.

### Can I get the old Google Assistant back?
On some devices and builds there's still a toggle in the Gemini app or a way to reassign the default assistant role, but Google is retiring Assistant, so treat any workaround as temporary. Availability varies by device, OS version and region, so check the official Google support pages for your handset instead of following a generic how-to.

### Does this happen with other assistants too?
Any assistant that routes a retrieval task through a generative model can hallucinate what it retrieved. The risk depends on how weakly the tool output is validated before it's spoken, not on which brand of model is behind it. Deterministic, non-LLM read-aloud paths such as accessibility screen readers don't have this failure mode at all.

### Is a hallucinated notification a privacy or data breach?
Usually not, because nothing was read that shouldn't have been. The failure is fabrication, not exposure: the assistant said something false instead of leaking something true. That distinction matters legally, and it's also why this kind of bug often slips past reviews that focus on data access rather than output accuracy.

### How do I stop an LLM from inventing items in a list I give it?
Never send an empty or partial list to the model in the first place. Set temperature to zero, enforce a JSON schema with an explicit item count, and validate the output against the source data before using it. If validation fails, fall back to deterministic formatting. The model should narrate facts, never supply them.
